stances.claim: Tetangco's defining virtue was not technical competence but nonpartisanship — his appointment by GMA and reappointment by Aquino III (who 'loathed the politics of his predecessor') is the best evidence of institutional objectivity transcending political loyalty.
stances.rhetorical_move: cross-partisan appointment as proof of institutional independence — using presidential hostility as the measure of nonpartisanship

stances.claim: The BSP's disciplinary firmness with erring banks is a model the judiciary should study to solve the perennial problem of delayed justice — with strict enforcement of constitutional time limits for resolving cases.
stances.rhetorical_move: cross-institutional lesson: banking regulation discipline as a template for judicial backlog reform

stances.claim: Heroism is complicated — Taruc's checkered life as Huk supremo and peasant advocate does not disqualify him from heroic status, consistent with the view that 'patriots are real people who lead complicated lives.'
stances.rhetorical_move: moral-complexity defense of contested heroism using Inquirer editorial and Nery column as co-witnesses
stances.confidence: asserted with personal distance ('to me he was a distant, self-appointed counselor')

notable_anecdotes: Taruc writing letters to CJ Panganiban in the late 1950s when he was president of FEUCSO and NUS, urging the 'former newsboy and bootblack' to lead the peasants — a politically sensitive personal detail disclosed with characteristic candor, establishing the intimacy of the radical-reformist temptation CJ resisted.

CJ's near-radicalization: he 'might have joined' Sison and Ocampo's Kabataang Makabayan had Alejandro Roces and Fr. Michael Nolan not persuaded him to instead organize and head the NUS as a counter to the KM — a biographical near-miss that reframes his entire subsequent legal-institutional career.
Romeo Taruc (Luis's son) being CJ's ally in student government and later his compadre — a cross-generational social bond that humanizes the Taruc-Panganiban connection beyond mere correspondence.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban profiles two contrasting 'supercitizens of Pampanga': the controversial Luis Taruc, posthumously declared a hero by the National Historical Commission, and the universally celebrated Amando Tetangco Jr., recently retired as BSP Governor. For Taruc, CJ discloses that as a late-1950s student leader (president of FEUCSO and NUS), he received letters from the Hukbalahap supremo urging the 'former newsboy and bootblack' to lead the peasants -- an appeal CJ acknowledges he 'might have' heeded had Alejandro Roces and Fr. Michael Nolan not persuaded him to organize the NUS as a counter to the Kabataang Makabayan of Sison and Ocampo. For Tetangco, CJ argues that his defining quality was not technical brilliance but nonpartisanship: his appointment by GMA and reappointment by Aquino III -- who 'loathed the politics of his predecessor' -- is the definitive proof that institutional integrity can transcend political cycles. CJ closes with two institutional observations: that the BSP, though created only by statute rather than by the Constitution, disciplines erring banks with a firmness the judiciary should emulate to solve case-delay problems; and that Tetangco's successor Espenilla, together with new Monetary Board members Favila and Abacan, signal continuity of the Duterte administration's laissez-faire approach to economic governance.
